scope: SCUMM engine games (MI1, MI2, Indiana Jones, DOTT, Sam & Max, etc.), Broken Sword 1 (sword1), Beneath a Steel Sky (sky), Flight of the Amazon Queen (queen), the gob games (Woodruff, Gobliiins) and the Discworld games (tinsel). The core tools — state / act / answer / walk / skip — and this wire protocol are shared across engines via a common bridge base (engines/mcp_bridge.*); each engine maps them onto its own world model.

scummvm.description: Connect to ScummVM's built-in MCP server. Enable by setting mcp=true in scummvm.ini. Use mcp_port to override the default port (23456).

notes: The MCP server uses Streamable HTTP (MCP spec 2025-03-26). Sync tools (state) return immediately; streaming tools (act, answer, walk, skip, and the game-specific tools) open an SSE channel and emit notifications as dialog plays out, then return a structured result when the action completes. The exact tool set and every tool's description are game-dependent — a game that never asks a dialog question has no answer tool, a game driven by a team of characters has a switch_character tool — and the optional settings add or remove tools too (mcp_skip_tool for skip, mcp_debug for the diagnostic set). Nothing that is not registered is ever referred to. Always query tools/list at runtime rather than assuming this document's list: it is a description of the shape, not of one game's surface. Beyond the core tools, some games expose extra tools (see gameTools).

initialize.description: Handshake. Client declares its protocol version; server replies with its capabilities and identity.

tools/list.description: List all MCP tools exposed by the engine.

tools.name: string
tools.description: string

tools/call.description: Invoke a tool. Sync tools (state) return immediately. Streaming tools (act, answer, walk, skip, and the game-specific tools) promote the connection to SSE and stream notifications before sending a final result.

params.name: string (core: state | act | answer | walk | skip; game-specific and debug tools listed under gameTools / debugTools — call tools/list for the live set)

tools.name: state
tools.description: Read the current game state: room, position, available verbs, inventory, visible objects, actors, buffered dialog lines, and any pending dialog question. Games add their own fields (e.g. a fist fight's gauges under 'fight'); read the outputSchema the server advertises for the running game.

verbs.description: Verb names currently available in the UI (e.g. walk_to, look_at, pick_up)

inventory.description: Names of items in the player's inventory

state_name.description: Human-readable state, present only for objects that have one (e.g. a door's "opened"/"closed", or the Monkey Island seagull's "eating"/"flying away"). Omitted otherwise. Localised to the game's language.

objects.description: Objects visible in the current room

actors.description: Names of actors present in the current room

messages.description: Dialog lines buffered since the last state call (cleared on read)

question.description: Present only when a dialog choice is pending. Use the answer tool to respond.

fight.description: Present only while a fist fight is on (games that have them). The verb bar is empty then and only the fight tool acts; the ordinary gameplay tools are refused until the fight ends.

tools.name: act
tools.description: Execute a verb on a named object or actor (by name or numeric ID from state). Streams SSE notifications as dialog plays out; returns a state-change summary when the action completes. For walking to pixel coordinates, use the walk tool instead.

verb.description: Verb to perform. Case-insensitive. Aliases: walk→walk_to, look→look_at, pick/pickup→pick_up, talk→talk_to.

oneOf.description: Primary target by name (from state.objects or state.actors)
Primary target by numeric object ID (from state.objects[].id)
Secondary target by name (for two-object verbs like use)
Secondary target by numeric object ID

examples.description: Walk to a named walk-box / hotspot
Talk to an actor, which returns a question with choices

choices.label: I want to be a pirate!

tools.name: answer
tools.description: Select a dialog choice by 1-based index. Only valid when state.question is present. Registered only for games that put questions to the player. Streams SSE notifications as the conversation plays out; returns a state-change summary when complete.

tools.name: walk
tools.description: Walk the player character to an explicit pixel coordinate. Out-of-bounds values are clamped to room bounds. Streams SSE notifications until the walk completes; returns a state-change summary.

x.description: Target X pixel coordinate (auto-clamped to [0, roomWidth-1])

y.description: Target Y pixel coordinate (auto-clamped to [0, roomHeight-1])

examples.note: Clamped to (roomWidth-1, 0) before the walk is issued

tools.name: skip
tools.description: Skip/cancel the current action or cutscene by simulating an Escape key press. Useful for skipping long intros or animations. Returns state changes.

gameTools.description: Tools registered only for specific games (in addition to the core tools). Always confirm availability via tools/list — they are absent for games that do not support them.

tools.name: play_note
tools.games: Loom; the Loom segment of Passport to Adventure
tools.description: Play Loom distaff notes. Accepts either {note:'c'} for one note, or {notes:['e','c','e','d']} to play a full sequence in one call. Only valid in the Loom segment (and full Loom). Note events played by the engine or the player are streamed as 'note' notifications.

note.description: Single note: one of c d e f g a b C (C is the high octave).

notes.description: Optional sequence of note strings to play in order, e.g. ['e','c','e','d'].

tools.name: fight
tools.games: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade; the Indy3 segment of Passport to Adventure
tools.description: Make a move in a fist fight. Accepts either {move:'punch_high'} for one move, or {moves:['block_high','punch_low']} to make several in a row. Punches and blocks come at three heights (a block only stops a punch at the same height) and step_back moves out of range; the bridge maps each move to the key that means it from the side the player is fighting from, so an agent never deals with the game's directional keypad. Valid only while a fight is on — state reports one under 'fight' — and refused outside one. While a fight is on the verb bar is empty and the ordinary gameplay tools (act, answer, walk, skip, play_note) are refused in turn, so fight is the only way to act; state stays available throughout. The result carries the fight gauges as they stand when the exchange resolves, or fight_over:true once the fight has ended.

moves.description: Optional sequence of move names to make in order, e.g. ['block_high','punch_low'].

tools.name: shoot_cannon
tools.games: The Curse of Monkey Island (cannon minigame)
tools.description: Aim the cannon at screen position (x, y) and fire a cannonball. The skeleton war-canoes to sink are listed in state as boat_N objects with their (x, y); aim at one of those points. Blocks until the shot resolves (flight, explosion, any resulting speech), then returns state changes; a sunk boat disappears from state.objects.

x.description: Screen X to aim at (0–639); pass a boat's x from state.objects.

y.description: Screen Y to aim at (0–479); pass a boat's y from state.objects.

tools.name: ride_bike
tools.description: Play the Full Throttle motorcycle minigame. Available once Ben has the bike keys (from the bartender) and is at his bike at the bar front. Mounts the bike and rides onto the highway; the Rottwheeler fight runs as a real-time action sequence which this tool auto-plays. Takes no arguments. Blocks until the section ends, then returns state changes.

tools.name: choose_kids
tools.description: Pick the three heroes on the title screen and start the game. Dave always leads the rescue, so name the two kids who join him (naming Dave as the third is accepted); the cast is dave, syd, michael, wendy, bernard, razor and jeff. Each portrait is clicked in turn and identified by the line the game prints for it, so the order the portraits are in does not matter, then START is pressed. Only valid while state reports kid_selection_pending. Blocks until the game has begun (by default escaping through the intro until the player has control) and returns state changes, with the team in 'kids'.

kids.description: The three heroes, by name: the two kids joining Dave, or all three with Dave named as well.

skip_intro.description: Escape through the opening cutscene so the call returns with the player already in control (default true).

tools.name: switch_character
tools.description: Switch the player-controlled kid (the F1–F3 keys). state lists the available names in 'available_characters' and the current one in 'controlling'. Only allowed during normal gameplay. Blocks until the switch settles, then returns state changes (room_changed/position reflect the newly controlled kid).

name.description: Name of the kid to control, as listed in state.available_characters (e.g. 'dave').

tools.name: dial
tools.description: Dial a number on the phone dial pad. Only valid while the dial pad is on screen (use the phone first via act(verb='use', target1='phone')). Presses the keypad buttons one at a time, blocks until the sequence (and any resulting call) settles, then returns state changes.

number.description: Number to dial, as a string of keypad keys: digits 0-9 plus '*' and '#' (e.g. '1234').

debugTools.description: Diagnostic tools, registered only when mcp_debug=true in the game's scummvm.ini section. Each declares an input and an output schema like every other tool; the debug read-out itself is deliberately open, since which sections a game keeps differs per game. keystroke/mouse_move/mouse_click are injected input and take effect on the next engine frame; they answer with what they injected, so read state (or take a screenshot) to see what came of it.

tools.name: debug
tools.description: Return raw engine state for diagnostics: room id, ego position, _userPut, _mouse, _virtualMouse, _leftBtnPressed, _rightBtnPressed, _mouseAndKeyboardStat, _keyPressed, _currentRoom, plus a slice of SCUMM script vars (0..127 by default).

from.description: First SCUMM var index to return (default 0).

to.description: Last SCUMM var index to return (inclusive, default 127).

tools.name: keystroke
tools.description: Inject a keyboard keystroke into the engine (sets _keyPressed for the next frame). Useful for skipping cutscenes, opening menus, or game-specific shortcuts (the numpad 1-9 keys drive the Indy3 boxing minigame).

key.description: A single ASCII character ('a','C','1') or a name ('Escape','Return','Space','Tab','Backspace','F1'..'F12','Up','Down','Left','Right').

tools.name: mouse_move
tools.description: Move the virtual mouse cursor to (x, y) in room/screen coordinates. Updates _mouse, _virtualMouse, and VAR_VIRT_MOUSE_X/Y. Does not click.

tools.name: mouse_click
tools.description: Simulate a mouse click at (x, y), processed like a real player click (walks ego, runs verb script, etc.). Button defaults to left; set 'double' for a double click.

double.description: True for a double click (two clicks within ~250ms). Default false.

tools.name: screenshot
tools.description: Return the current frame as a PNG image, and by default also write it to the configured screenshot folder (auto-numbered, like the in-app screenshot key). The image comes back as an MCP image content block (base64 PNG) alongside the structured result {width, height, saved}, so a client can simply look at the game.

save_to_disk.description: Also write the frame to the screenshot folder (default true).

tools.name: save_state
tools.description: Save the current game to a save slot, the same way the in-game save menu does. Writes <target>.s<NN> in the active save path, so it can capture reusable save states for tests. Returns the slot and whether the save was accepted.

description.description: Optional label stored in the save header (default "mcp save").

tools.name: set_talk_speed
tools.description: Force the game's text/talk speed at runtime on the 0..255 scale used by --talkspeed (0 = slowest, 255 = fastest, instant text). Needed for titles whose boot script overrides the configured talkspeed (e.g. the Fate of Atlantis demo). Updates ConfMan and the live VAR_CHARINC.

speed.description: Talk speed on the 0..255 scale (0 = slowest, 255 = fastest).

stateChanges.description: State changes that occurred while the action ran

messages.description: Dialog lines spoken during the action

room_changed.description: New room number (only present if the room changed)

question.description: Present if a dialog choice is pending after the action

fight.description: Fist-fight gauges as they stand once the exchange resolved (games with fights only): {indy:{health,punch_power}, opponent:{health,punch_power}}

fight_over.description: True when the fight that was on has ended (games with fights only)

scumm.coordinates: Room/screen pixel coordinates, in every SCUMM version. V0-V2 (Maniac Mansion, Zak McKracken) keep actors and objects on a compressed grid internally (x/8, y/2); the bridge converts, so state.position, object x/y and walk(x, y) are all plain room pixels there too.
scumm.verbs: Per-game verb bar (or a fixed fallback set for single-cursor games), reported in state.verbs. V3-V5 label their slots with text; V6+ moved to image verbs, except Day of the Tentacle, which kept the text bar (its 'Look at' label is rewritten from the game font's ligature glyph to plain text, and 'walk to' is exposed even though DOTT dropped its button).
scumm.objects: state.objects carries id, name, state/state_name, compatible_verbs, pathway. Room-to-room exits are often nameless hotspots in the game data (all of Maniac Mansion's are); those are listed as 'pathway_<id>' with pathway=true, and act(verb='walk to', target1=<that name or id>) goes through them.
scumm.names: A name is whatever the game itself would print for the thing, normalized (lower case, spaces as underscores). Two details show up in Fate of Atlantis: a name the game writes as a message rather than as text is resolved first, so the orichalcum beads read as their live count ('3_beads'); and a scene that names several things alike (the Lost Kingdom's seven cave mouths are all 'cave') has them numbered in id order ('cave_1'..'cave_7'), with the bare name still answering with the first of them. An action's inventory_added/inventory_removed/objects_changed report the same names state does, so a name just reported can be passed straight back to act.
scumm.clickOnlyScreens: Monkey Island 2 hides its verb bar on the island maps and once Guybrush is in the swamp coffin: the sentence line names the only action ("row to"), and a click is the whole interface. state reports that verb and offers it on every object; act(verb, target1) and walk(x, y) replay the click, so travelling on the map switches room and rowing moves the coffin.
scumm.lookAt: In V0-V2 (Maniac Mansion, Zak McKracken) the bar's 'What is' verb only names an object: the interpreter never runs a sentence for it, it writes the name into the sentence line. act(verb='what is', target1=…) answers with that name as a message and changes nothing else — there are no descriptions to read in these games.
scumm.extraTools: Game-specific: play_note, fight, shoot_cannon, ride_bike, choose_kids, switch_character, dial (the phone keypad close-up, in both Maniac Mansion and Zak McKracken). Debug adds set_talk_speed.
scumm.backgroundSpeech: A room can talk to itself with the player in full control (Zak's living-room TV prints a line every few seconds). Pre-V7 games stop waiting on speech once the action itself has been finished for a short while, so such a room does not make every action time out; the lines are still captured and arrive with the next state call.
scumm.fights: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (and its segment in Passport to Adventure) puts the player in fist fights, which suspend the whole interface: the verb bar empties, nothing is selectable and the game reads only its own fighting keys. state reports the fight under 'fight' (each fighter's health and punch-power gauge), the fight tool makes the moves, and act/answer/walk/skip/play_note are refused with an error naming the fight until it ends — so an agent is never left sending actions the game silently drops.

sword-family.scope: Broken Sword 1 (sword1). The contract is written to extend to Broken Sword 2 (sword2) unchanged; only the engine adapter differs.
sword-family.interface: One-click game: a left click runs an object's interaction script, a right click looks at it. There is no verb bar.
sword-family.verbs: A fixed set, always: look_at (right click), and interact / use / talk_to / pick_up (all left click), plus walk_to. state.verbs advertises it.
sword-family.coordinates: World (compact) coordinates everywhere — the space of the compacts' o_xcoord/o_ycoord and mouse boxes, and of scriptVars MOUSE_X/MOUSE_Y. Scroll-invariant. Screen coordinates appear only inside debug.
sword-family.objectNaming: Broken Sword attaches no name to a scene object, so the bridge ships naming tables and every unnamed compact falls back to 'object_<section>_<index>', derived from its (fixed) compact id. That fallback is a first-class target: act accepts it, a raw decimal id, an 0x-prefixed hex id, an authored name, or an inventory item name.
sword-family.objects: state.objects carries id, name, kind (floor/character/object/hotspot), position (mouse-box centre) and box ([x1,y1,x2,y2], inclusive). The player is excluded and reported as state.position ({x,y,dir}).
sword-family.inventory: state.inventory carries name, pocket number and, when the game provides one, a description (the item's own text).
sword-family.canAct: state.can_act is false while the game is not accepting input (cutscene, fade, control panel); act/walk/answer are rejected until it is true.
sword-family.question: A pending conversation is the subject bar: state.question.choices are its topics; answer(id) picks the 1-based slot.
sword-family.walk: walk(x,y) drives the floor compact under (x,y); a point on no floor returns a validation error listing the screen's floor boxes.
sword-family.debug: The debug tool (mcp_debug) has sections vars / compacts / pockets / system; 'compacts' is the dump used to author the object-name tables.

sky.interface: Two-button game with no verb bar: one button examines a hotspot, the other walks Foster there and runs its interaction script. The bridge dispatches every action by replaying real input — it warps the engine's virtual cursor and presses a button, and the game's own mouse engine does the rest.
sky.verbs: A fixed set, always: look_at (examine button), and interact / use / talk_to / pick_up (action button), plus walk_to. state.verbs advertises it.
sky.coordinates: Game (compact) coordinates everywhere — the space of Compact::xcood/ycood and the mouse hit boxes. The visible play area spans (128,136)..(447,327). Screen coordinates appear only inside the debug tools.
sky.objectNaming: Names come from the game's own data: an object's cursorText string (the label the game shows on hover — these are live, so examining the junk pile can rename it to robot_shell) with the authored compact name as fallback, normalized and de-duplicated (door, door_2). Floors are all named 'floor'.
sky.objects: state.objects carries id (compact id), name, kind (floor/character/hotspot), position (hit-box centre) and box ([x1,y1,x2,y2]). Foster is excluded and reported as state.position ({x,y,dir}).
sky.inventory: state.inventory lists the items the game's icon bar would show (name + compact id). act on an inventory item is played out through the real icon bar: the bridge holds the cursor on the top line until the bar drops, clicks the icon (arming OBJECT_HELD), then clicks the second target.
sky.canAct: state.can_act mirrors the engine's own mouse gate (MOUSE_STATUS/MOUSE_STOP); act/walk are rejected while it is false (scripted sequence in progress).
sky.question: A pending conversation is the text chooser: state.question.choices are the on-screen options, top to bottom; answer(id) clicks the 1-based choice.
sky.walk: walk(x,y) clicks the floor compact under (x,y); a point on no floor returns a validation error listing the screen's floor boxes.
sky.debug: The debug tool (mcp_debug) has sections vars / compacts / compact:<id> / system; 'compacts' dumps the current screen's mouse list with names and hit boxes.

queen.interface: Verb-panel game (open/close/move/give/use/pick up/talk to/look at). act maps one-to-one onto the game's own command machinery: the bridge builds the finished command (verb + subjects in the panel's encoding) and the engine executes it exactly as a mouse-built sentence — including walking Joe over, cutaways and dialogues.
queen.verbs: The panel set, always: open, close, move, give, use, pick_up, talk_to, look_at, plus walk_to. 'interact' is accepted as an alias for use. state.verbs advertises it.
queen.coordinates: Room pixel coordinates (320x200 with the room area above y=150). walk(x,y) walks Joe to a room position.
queen.objectNaming: Names come from the game's own object-name table, normalized, stripped of control characters and de-duplicated (sheets, sheets_2). The game renames objects as their state changes (sheets becomes other_sheet, the radiator becomes radiator_with_sheet_rope).
queen.objects: state.objects carries id (room-relative object number), name, kind (object/person), pathway (true for exits), position (authored x/y when present) and default_verb (the object's own default action). Joe is reported as state.position.
queen.inventory: state.inventory lists every carried item (name + item number).
queen.canAct: state.can_act is false during cutaways and dialogues; act/walk are rejected until it is true.
queen.question: A pending conversation is the sentence chooser at the bottom of the screen: state.question.choices are the options on offer; answer(id) selects the 1-based displayed sentence (the same mapping as the keyboard digit shortcuts).
queen.changes: objects_changed reports objects that became visible or hidden during an action ({name, old_state, new_state} with visible/hidden), which is how silent scene changes (moving the curtain revealing the wig) surface.
queen.debug: The debug tool (mcp_debug) has sections gamestate / objects / items / system.

woodruff.scope: The Bizarre Adventures of Woodruff and the Schnibble (gob engine).
woodruff.interface: Script-driven, one-click point-and-click game: no verb bar and no object model, just rectangular hotspots. One click on a hotspot is the whole interaction — the game walks Woodruff over and runs the hotspot's script itself — so act sends exactly one, for scenery, characters and exits alike. The bridge dispatches every action by replaying real cursor input: it moves the cursor onto the target, waits for the game to register the hover (entering a hotspot runs its enter() handler, which is what tells the scripts what is being pointed at), and only then presses. Clicking without that hover makes the game act on the previously pointed-at hotspot, which shows up as the action playing out without Woodruff walking there.
woodruff.verbs: A fixed set, always: interact (the default click) and use, plus walk_to. There is no separate look verb — interact examines, talks, opens and picks up as the target dictates. pick_up / open / close / talk_to / push / pull are accepted as interact aliases. state.verbs advertises it.
woodruff.coordinates: Game pixel coordinates (the 640x480 hotspot/cursor space; scroll and screen offsets are applied internally). walk(x,y) clicks the floor at that point. Screen coordinates appear only inside the debug tools.
woodruff.objectNaming: Names come from the game's own status-bar text: the bridge parks the cursor on each hotspot (a hover sweep) to capture the name the game draws, then turns it into a stable identifier (lower-cased, spaces to underscores, leading article stripped — English a/an/the and French un/une/le/la/les). The game's text is in the DOS OEM code page (CP850) even in the Windows release, so it is decoded to UTF-8 first: labels keep their accents ('Un recueil de détritus') and identifiers fold them to ASCII ('recueil_de_detritus'). Exits keep their 'to_...'/'vers_...' form and are flagged as pathways. Unnamed hotspots fall back to hotspot_<id>. naming_pending is true while a fresh screen is still being swept.
woodruff.objects: state.objects carries id (hotspot id), name, label (the raw status-bar text, in the game's own language), position (rect centre x/y) and pathway (true for exits). Woodruff himself is listed as an object (woodruff).
woodruff.inventory: state.inventory lists carried items (name + label + slot id). No save support, so items are learned live: after every action the bridge opens the game's own inventory overlay, reads the item names the overlay draws, and closes it again.
woodruff.use: 'use <item> on <target>' selects the inventory item onto the cursor through the real overlay, then clicks the target (Woodruff walks over first). target1 is matched against the inventory only for use, so a world object sharing an item's name stays reachable with interact.
woodruff.canAct: state.can_act is false while an action, walk or cutscene is playing out; act/walk are rejected until the game is waiting for input again.
woodruff.question: This game has no MCP dialog chooser: conversations play as scripted lines surfaced in messages, so answer is not used.
woodruff.skip: The game has no save states; skip breaks the intro videos one at a time. Once the game is interactive skip is rejected with "nothing to skip", which is the done signal for an intro-skip loop.
woodruff.debug: The debug tool (mcp_debug) has sections system / hotspots / text_items / vars, plus screenshot / mouse_move / mouse_click / keystroke.

gobliiins.scope: Gobliiins (gob engine) — the games driven by a team of three characters.
gobliiins.interface: No verb bar, no hover text and no per-object click zone: the whole picture is one zone, and what a click does is decided by the cursor, which the player cycles with the other mouse button through three settings — go to the spot, use the controlling character's own ability there, or take what is there. The bridge reports the game's own tables instead of the screen's click zones (the three characters and the scene objects) and replays exactly that input for every action: it cycles the cursor to what the verb means, moves it onto the point, lets the game register it, then clicks.
gobliiins.verbs: Three, and each of them is a different cursor: 'walk to' only goes to the spot, 'interact' uses the ability that character alone has on whatever is there, and 'pick up' takes what is there — or puts down what is being carried. open / close / talk_to / push / pull / use are accepted as aliases of interact. There is no look verb: the game answers by doing.
gobliiins.targets: act takes either target1 (a name from state.objects) or a plain x/y. Coordinates are the usual way to point at something: most of the picture is scenery that no object covers. Out-of-screen coordinates are refused rather than clamped.
gobliiins.characters: state.characters lists the three team members with their position and whether they can be taken over; state.controlling names the one act and walk drive. switch_character hands control over by name (or to the next one when called with no name), and is refused while the current character is mid-action or standing somewhere they may not be left. Each has an ability the others lack, so the puzzle is usually choosing who acts.
gobliiins.objects: state.objects carries id, name (object_<id>), the centre of its rectangle (x/y) and pickable when it can be carried away. The names are positional identifiers: the game paints no names for a player either.
gobliiins.inventory: One item at a time: state.inventory holds the carried item (item_<id>) or nothing. Taking it and putting it down are the same verb, 'pick up', and carrying it is what changes what interact does.
gobliiins.canAct: state.can_act is false while a video or scripted sequence is playing; act, walk and switch_character are rejected until the game is waiting for input again. An action's stream stays open until the character has stopped moving, so the position it returns is where they ended up.
gobliiins.question: This game asks no dialog questions, so answer is never used.
gobliiins.skip: The demo has no save states; skip breaks the intro videos one at a time. Once the game is interactive skip is rejected with "nothing to skip", which is the done signal for an intro-skip loop.
gobliiins.screenshots: Because names are positional here, the screenshot tool (mcp_debug) is the natural companion: it returns the frame as an image, which is how to tell what an object_<id> actually is.

discworld.interface: Pointer game with no verb bar: the vocabulary is which button was pressed over what — a single left click walks there, a double left click is the action, a right click looks. act maps onto those three. What the game acts on is not a coordinate but whatever its own tag process last latched onto, so the bridge parks the cursor on the target, lets a few frames pass, and then raises the same player event the keyboard bindings raise.
discworld.verbs: Always three: walk_to, look_at, use. interact / pick_up / talk_to / open / close / push / pull / give are accepted as aliases for use, since the target itself decides what the action is.
discworld.coordinates: Scene coordinates — 320x200 in the first game, 640x480 in the second — and the scene is often wider than the screen. walk(x, y) clamps to the scene.
discworld.objectNaming: Names are the labels the game paints next to the cursor, folded into identifiers (lower case, spaces as underscores, punctuation dropped) and de-duplicated (door, door_2). Something the game never labels is still targetable, as object_<n> / exit_<n> / actor_<n>.
discworld.objects: state.objects carries id, name, kind (character for a tagged actor, scenery for a tag/exit polygon), x/y (the spot the bridge points at) and pathway=true when going there leaves the scene. The player character is state.position and is never listed.
discworld.inventory: state.inventory lists every carried item with its id, and marks the one in hand with held=true (also state.held_item). Nothing in the game data maps an item to a name — the game only says what an item is by running that item's own script when the player points at it — so the bridge asks each item's script for its name while the game is idle and publishes what it prints. An item not yet asked reads as item_<id>.
discworld.itemsOnThings: An action is carried out with whatever is in hand. act(verb='use', target1=<thing>, target2=<item>) puts the named carried item in hand first, which is how one thing is used on another; either target may be the item.
discworld.canAct: state.can_act is false while a scene is playing itself out, while a movie runs and while a conversation is waiting for an answer; act/walk are rejected until it is true.
discworld.question: A conversation is an icon window rather than lines of text: state.question.choices are the options it is offering (named the same way inventory items are), and the last choice always ends the conversation. answer(id) picks one.
discworld.changes: objects_changed reports things that appeared or vanished within the scene ({name, old_state, new_state} with present/absent) — opening the wardrobe revealing the pouch. held_item reports the item in hand after the action when it changed (empty string when the hand was emptied), and room_name accompanies room_changed.
discworld.skip: skip presses Escape, which is what cuts an escapable sequence short and what stops a movie. It reports what that one press did rather than waiting for the game to hand control back, which it may not do for several scenes yet.
discworld.debug: The debug tool (mcp_debug) has sections system / objects / items.
